title: Optimal branching angle has cosine equal to ratio of energy loss in trunk and branch

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Optimal branching angle has cosine equal to ratio of energy loss in trunk and branch

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The most favourable angle at which an arterial branch leaves its trunk is that whose cosine equals the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel to that in the branch (cos x = L/L′).

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: \cos x = L/L', L and L' the energy loss per unit length in trunk and branch

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: That is to say, the most favourable angle of branching will be such that the cosine of the angle is equal to the ratio of the loss of energy which the blood undergoes, per unit of length, in the main vessel, as compared with that which it undergoes in the branch.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XV, “On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures”; topic “Branching of arteries”. Scope: arterial branching in vertebrates

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: \cos x = L/L', L and L' the energy loss per unit length in trunk and branch

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch15-15: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The equation is explicit and discriminating. Geometry is public, but the branch-resolved in vivo flow and loss measurements needed across vertebrate arteries are generally absent, making a direct test data-limited.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each bifurcation, estimate energy loss per unit length in trunk and branch from matched geometry and flow, and compare observed angle with arccos(L/L′). Persistent deviations beyond measurement error would refute the law.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Pulsatile non-Newtonian flow complicates L and L′.

Matched local energy losses and branch angles are rarely available.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The cosine formula is explicit, and angles plus radii are in open reconstructions. Turning those radii into Thompson's energy loss per unit length requires a flow model, and Vascular Model Repository simulations cover only a subset of vessels. The resulting comparison can check consistency with the formula and struggles to separate it from other radius-based angle rules.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each branch, compare the observed angle with arccos of the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the parent and in the branch. Support would be a tight match between that predicted angle and the measured angle; systematic deviation toward a size-only or constant-angle rule would refute the energy-loss formula.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Energy loss is usually inferred from radius and assumed flow, so the test can recycle the same hydraulic assumptions that motivate the formula.

Local pressure-drop measurements paired with angles are uncommon outside simulated models.
